title: Sandbox management for AI coding agents: Common use cases and best practices for automated lifecycles
summary: How to manage AI coding agent sandboxes: microVM isolation, deny-by-default egress, secrets injection, and automated lifecycle policies.
body_markdown:
Your[coding agent](https://blaxel.ai/blog/how-do-ai-agents-execute-code.html) works fine in staging. It clones a repository, reads an issue, installs dependencies, and runs the tests. Then a pull request arrives with one hidden instruction in the README, and the agent follows it.


Indirect prompt injection is the main threat to coding agents. A sandbox limits the damage when an attack succeeds. But the sandbox boundary isn't the whole story. In July 2026, the Cloud Security Alliance published a[research note](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-ai-coding-agent-sandbox-escapes-20260722-c) on Pillar Security's sandbox-escape findings against widely used coding agents. Its summary: "the agent did not need to break the sandbox directly. It only had to write something that a trusted component outside the sandbox would later run."


Coding agents also execute more code per task than they used to. Agents now write scripts that call tools, instead of making one tool call at a time. Every task runs more[untrusted code](https://blaxel.ai/blog/run-untrusted-llm-generated-code-safely) , and that volume makes agent sandbox management a production requirement.


Isolation alone doesn't cover this. A production sandbox needs managed boundaries for network access, credentials, outputs, and lifetime. Without them, one poisoned input becomes a leaked secret, and a forgotten sandbox holds your source code for months. If you sell a coding agent to enterprises, these gaps surface in security reviews and stall deals.


This guide covers agent sandbox management for AI coding agents. You'll learn how to isolate workloads, control network access and credentials, handle outputs, and automate the lifecycle. It ends with the build-versus-buy decision.


## TL;DR


- **Isolate with**[microVMs](https://blaxel.ai/blog/serverless-vs-containers-vs-micro-vms-ai-agents) **:** AI-generated code is untrusted. Run each agent in its own microVM, a lightweight virtual machine with a dedicated kernel.
- **Deny egress by default:** Allowlist the domains each agent needs. Block everything else at the platform level.
- **Keep credentials outside:** Inject secrets through a proxy so sandbox code never sees raw API keys.
- **Distrust sandbox outputs:** Treat every file, hook, and config an agent writes as untrusted until reviewed.
- **Automate the lifecycle:** Suspend idle sandboxes, expire abandoned ones with time-to-live (TTL) policies, and log from outside the guest.


## Why AI coding agents need managed sandboxes


Agent sandbox management means the controls that govern a[sandbox environment](https://blaxel.ai/blog/what-is-a-sandbox-environment) from creation to deletion: hardware-enforced isolation, network and credential limits, handling of everything the agent produces, and lifecycle policies for suspension and expiry. For an[AI agent sandbox](https://blaxel.ai/blog/ai-sandbox) that runs code the model wrote, these controls decide how much damage a successful attack does.


Treat every line of LLM-generated code as untrusted. The[NVIDIA AI red team](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/how-code-execution-drives-key-risks-in-agentic-ai-systems) found that executing LLM-generated code without isolation leads to[remote code execution](https://blaxel.ai/blog/ai-runtime-security) . It also found that filtering or blocking dangerous commands provides only limited defense, because attacker-controlled context can make malicious activities appear legitimate. Containment holds where sanitization can only guess.


Security reviewers now ask about this directly. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) covers CVE-2025-59528 in its[Q1 2026 exploit round-up](https://genai.owasp.org/2026/04/14/owasp-genai-exploit-round-up-report-q1-2026) . The round-up maps this CustomMCP remote code execution flaw to ASI05, Unexpected Code Execution, in the Agentic Top 10. The listed mitigations were sandbox execution and restricted outbound connectivity. When your enterprise prospect's security team asks how you handle ASI05, "we run it in a container" is no longer a passing answer.


The volume of code per task is rising too. Anthropic's code-execution pattern has agents write scripts that call[Model Context Protocol (MCP)](https://blaxel.ai/blog/mcp-use-cases) tools instead of issuing one tool call at a time. Anthropic reports that this approach[can significantly reduce token usage](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/code-execution-with-mcp) compared with direct tool calls. The practical effect for you is more agent-written code running per session, which means more untrusted execution inside each sandbox.


A managed sandbox gives you four things a[bare runtime](https://blaxel.ai/blog/ai-agent-runtime-environment.html) doesn't:


- **Blast-radius containment:** A compromised agent reaches its own sandbox and the destinations you allowlisted, nothing else.
- **Hard resource limits:** CPU, memory, disk I/O, and bandwidth caps stop a runaway loop from becoming a denial of service for other tenants.
- **Audit trail:** Every tool call, process start, and network attempt is recorded outside the guest for incident response.
- **Compliance evidence:**[SOC 2](https://blaxel.ai/blog/soc-2-compliance-ai-guide.html) and require documented safeguards for sensitive data, but they do not generally mandate a specific documented isolation control for every system; HIPAA expressly requires isolation of health care clearinghouse functions in certain organizational contexts. A managed platform's controls become part of your evidence.


The five controls below follow the path an attack takes: code, network, credentials, outputs, detection. Lifecycle policies then limit how long any of it stays exposed.


## How to secure a sandbox for AI coding agents


Agent sandboxing for coding agents comes down to five controls. The order matters because it mirrors how an attack travels: a malicious instruction lands in code, the code reaches for the network, it looks for credentials, it writes artifacts for trusted tools to run, and you detect it or you don't. Each control ends with a next step you can hand to your platform team this week.


### 1. Isolate each agent in its own microVM


Containers are the industry standard for running your own trusted software in[multi-tenant](https://blaxel.ai/blog/tenant-isolation) settings. AI-generated code is neither yours nor trusted. For that workload, microVMs give each sandbox its own guest kernel behind a hardware virtualization boundary. An exploit inside one sandbox stops at that boundary instead of reaching the host or a neighboring tenant.


Container escape vulnerabilities like[CVE-2024-21626](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-21626) show the exposure. When workloads share a kernel layer, the patch cadence of that layer becomes your risk. Alternatives exist.[GKE Agent Sandbox](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/machine-learning/agent-sandbox) uses gVisor, a user-space kernel that intercepts system calls. gVisor improves on plain containers, but it remains a software interposition layer rather than a hardware boundary. Full virtualization costs little. The[Firecracker paper](https://assets.amazon.science/96/c6/302e527240a3b1f86c86c3e8fc3d/firecracker-lightweight-virtualization-for-serverless-applications.pdf) reports boot times under 125 milliseconds per microVM, with a memory footprint[under 5 MiB](https://firecracker-microvm.github.io/) . Boot is a one-time cost per sandbox, distinct from resuming an existing sandbox, which the lifecycle section covers.


Approach Kernel Boundary Fit for AI-generated code


Containers Shared host kernel Software, OS-level Trusted code only


gVisor User-space kernel System call interception Better, still software


MicroVMs Dedicated guest kernel Hardware virtualization Required


Enforce CPU, memory, disk I/O, and bandwidth quotas outside the guest. Root inside the microVM can't lift a limit the hypervisor applies. A memory leak in agent-written code kills that one sandbox instead of the host.


**Next step:** Set per-sandbox limits at creation. Run a script that deliberately leaks memory and confirm the platform kills the sandbox, not the host. For the escape mechanics behind this control, see our guide to[container escapes](https://blaxel.ai/blog/container-escape) .


### 2. Deny network egress by default


A coding agent needs a handful of destinations: the package registry, your git host, the model API, and an internal artifact store. Allowlist those per agent and block everything else. Resolve DNS through resolvers you control, since an open resolver is itself an exfiltration channel. Enforce the policy outside the guest. A firewall the agent can reach from inside is a policy the agent can disable with root. Suppose a prompt injection tells the agent to post your` .env` to an attacker's domain. The connection fails at the platform layer before any bytes leave.


The OWASP guidance above pairs restricted outbound connectivity with sandbox execution for a reason. Isolation without egress control contains the code but not the data. Tight allowlists also reduce approval fatigue. Cursor reports that sandboxing cut how often its agents stop to ask for permission[by 40%](https://cursor.com/blog/agent-sandboxing) . For your team, that means fewer interruptions and fewer rubber-stamped approvals.


**Next step:** Run in a logging-only mode for a week and record every blocked request. Then promote the legitimate destinations to the allowlist and switch to enforcement. The full pattern set, including domain allowlisting and DNS control, is in our[deny-by-default guide](https://blaxel.ai/blog/egress-control-deny-by-default-ai-agents) .


### 3. Keep secrets outside the sandbox


Sandbox code should call an API without holding the key. A proxy outside the sandbox attaches the credential server-side, and only for hosts on the allowlist. A compromised agent that dumps environment variables, reads mounted files, or searches the filesystem finds nothing worth stealing. The egress allowlist from control 2 and the proxy work together: approved destinations get credentials, and only the proxy knows them.


Start each sandbox with an empty credential set. Some code genuinely needs a token inside the guest, such as a git push. For those cases, issue a short-lived, task-scoped token from a broker and let it expire with the task. Long-lived keys baked into images or injected at boot are the pattern to retire. Once inside the guest, they're readable by whatever the agent runs, and a single injected instruction can read them.


**Next step:** Audit your sandbox images and environment configs for long-lived keys. Replace each with proxy injection or a task-scoped token. Verify by running` env` and a filesystem search inside a live sandbox and confirming nothing sensitive comes back.


### 4. Treat everything that leaves the sandbox as untrusted


The escapes described in the intro share one mechanism. An agent writes a git hook, a task-runner config, a` .cursorrules` or` AGENT.md` instruction file, or an interpreter config. A trusted tool outside the sandbox, such as your IDE, a CI runner, or a merge pipeline, then runs it. NVIDIA's[sandboxing guidance](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/practical-security-guidance-for-sandboxing-agentic-workflows-and-managing-execution-risk) makes the same point: hooks, MCP configs, and skill scripts often run outside the sandbox.


Honest scoping matters here. In the cases described, the trusted tools appear to have shared a workstation with the sandbox. Remote microVMs remove the workstation from the equation. But CI, preview servers, git hooks, and merge pipelines that consume sandbox output are the same boundary in a different place. OWASP's[Secure Coding with AI](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secure_Coding_with_AI_Cheat_Sheet.html) cheat sheet flags continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) agents for exactly this confused-deputy risk.


Block writes outside the project workspace and to tool configuration files unless a human reviews them. Agents install dependencies, so pin versions and scan lockfiles before anything downstream installs from them.


**Next step:** Put a review or policy gate between sandbox output and any system that holds credentials. If a file the agent wrote can trigger execution in CI, it needs the same scrutiny as a pull request from a stranger.


### 5. Log from outside the guest and contain automatically


Log tool calls, process starts, network attempts (allowed and denied), and[resource usage](https://blaxel.ai/blog/ai-observability.html) at the platform layer. Hypervisor-level capture is more resistant to tampering by code running in the guest than guest-side monitoring. Retain the logs in write-once storage so an attacker with sandbox access can't edit the timeline. That record is also what your incident response and compliance audits run on.


Track[lifecycle latency](https://blaxel.ai/blog/sub-second-sandbox-startup-2026) alongside security events so you can verify sandbox behavior in your own stack instead of relying only on advertised figures. Kubernetes Agent Sandbox exposes Prometheus histograms for suspend, resume, and restore latency:


Lifecycle signal What it verifies


Create latency Time from the creation request until the sandbox is interactive


` sandbox_client_suspend_latency_ms` Time required to move an active sandbox into standby


` sandbox_client_resume_latency_ms` Time required to resume a standby sandbox


` sandbox_client_restore_latency_ms` Time required to restore a sandbox from saved state


Stream platform logs to the same external pipeline as these metrics, including stdout, stderr, lifecycle transitions, process starts, and denied network requests. Correlate every record with the sandbox, tenant, task, and timestamp so an investigation can reconstruct what happened before and after a suspend, resume, or restore.


Baselines turn logs into alerts. For example, an agent making 500 API calls in one minute instead of its normal 10 to 20 trips an alert, and investigation often points to an injected instruction enumerating a database. The containment order is:


1. **Terminate:** Kill the microVM.
2. **Snapshot:** Capture its state for forensics.
3. **Alert:** Page the security team.


The whole sequence should finish within seconds of detection, before meaningful data leaves.


Together, the five controls answer the questions on an enterprise security questionnaire. Reviewers ask how code is isolated, where it can connect, and where keys live. They also ask what happens to its output and how you know when something goes wrong. A gap in any one becomes a finding, and findings extend sales cycles.


**Next step:** Define three alert rules before go-live: spikes in egress denials, process trees that don't match the agent's normal tooling, and API call volume outside the per-task baseline.


## How to automate the sandbox lifecycle


Lifecycle is where cost, security, and speed trade off. Always-on sandboxes mean paying for compute between sessions, even when the agent is waiting on a human. Ephemeral sandboxes mean re-cloning the repository and reinstalling dependencies every session. That repeated setup adds wait time and discards state the agent built. The two controls below handle idle sandboxes and abandoned ones, which are different problems.


### Suspend idle sandboxes instead of deleting them


Agent infrastructure platforms like Blaxel move an idle sandbox to[standby](https://blaxel.ai/platform/sandboxes) seconds after network activity stops. It resumes in under 25ms with filesystem, memory and running processes intact. Standby carries no compute charge; you pay only for snapshot and volume storage. Blaxel's documentation notes that external network connections go stale across standby. Database sessions, queue consumers, and HTTP pools need reconnecting on resume.


Under 25ms sits well below the delay users perceive as a pause.


Delty, a pull request (PR) review agent, runs[isolated PR reviews](https://blaxel.ai/blog/delty-builds-secure-high-context-ai-pull-request-reviews-with-blaxel-sandboxes) for enterprise customers on sandboxes that resume in 25ms.


Standby is not a durable-storage guarantee. Use Volumes for data that must survive sandbox deletion, or Agent Drive, currently in private preview, for co-located shared storage across agents and sessions. Stateless agents that run one command and return a result don't need standby at all; create, execute, and delete. For the implementation details of each state, see[sandbox lifecycle states](https://blaxel.ai/blog/understand-the-lifecycle-of-a-blaxel-sandbox) .


### Expire abandoned sandboxes with TTL policies


Standby fixes[idle cost](https://blaxel.ai/blog/ai-agent-development-costs) . It doesn't fix accumulated risk. NVIDIA's sandboxing guidance warns that long-running sandboxes accumulate stale artifacts and cached credentials, which raises what an attacker gains from compromising one. A sandbox nobody has touched in months still holds your source code, your dependency cache, and whatever tokens the agent fetched along the way.


Blaxel lets you set[TTL and expiration policies](https://docs.blaxel.ai/Sandboxes/Expiration.md) when you create a sandbox. Starter quota tiers[enforce a maximum TTL](https://docs.blaxel.ai/Sandboxes/Overview) , so starter-tier sandboxes can't live forever by accident.


Give trial tenants a short idle TTL, for example a day. Give paying tenants a longer idle window plus a maximum age. Move anything worth keeping into a Volume first, since deleted sandboxes can't be recovered.


**Next step:** Set a default expiration policy at creation for each tenant tier. Then list every running sandbox with no policy attached and assign one.


## Build vs buy: what self-managed sandbox infrastructure involves


Building your own[sandbox infrastructure](https://blaxel.ai/blog/sandbox-provider-security-assessment-checklist.html) fits three situations. They are air-gapped requirements ruling out managed clouds, unusual hardware, or a platform team already running Firecracker in production. Outside those, you're signing up to own six systems that aren't your product:


- **Isolation-layer patching:** Tracking hypervisor and guest kernel vulnerabilities and rolling fixes across every host.
- **Snapshot and restore:** Capturing memory and filesystem state, storing it, and restoring it fast enough that agents stay interactive.
- **Egress proxy:** Per-agent allowlists, DNS control, and logging of denied requests.
- **Secrets injection:** A proxy that attaches credentials server-side and a broker that issues task-scoped tokens.
- **Audit logging:** Hypervisor-level capture of tool calls, processes, and network attempts in write-once storage.
- **Lifecycle automation:** Idle detection, standby, expiration policies, and cleanup that never leaves orphaned environments.


Expect one to two infrastructure engineers for six months or more before the first agent runs on it, then an on-call rotation afterward. Those engineers aren't shipping agent features during that time, and the configuration they produce has to be maintained by whoever inherits it.


Three questions settle the decision:


1. **Is sandbox infrastructure your product's differentiator?** If customers buy your agent for what it does, not for how it's isolated, the infrastructure is a cost center.
2. **Do compliance needs require your own hosting?** SOC 2 auditors and HIPAA programs generally accept a provider's attested controls as part of your evidence. For HIPAA, add a business associate agreement (BAA) with the provider.
3. **Can you staff on-call for isolation incidents?** A container escape at 2 AM needs someone who knows the hypervisor layer.


Three "no" answers point to buying. One "yes" on question two deserves a conversation about private networking options before you commit to building.

## FAQs about sandbox management


### What is the difference between containers and microVMs for AI agent sandboxes?


The difference is the kernel. Containers share the host kernel, so a kernel vulnerability exposes every workload on that host. MicroVMs run each workload on its own guest kernel behind a hardware virtualization boundary. Containers remain the right default for running your own trusted software in multi-tenant settings. For AI-generated or otherwise untrusted code, microVMs are the boundary that holds when the code inside is fully compromised.


### How does lifecycle management reduce sandbox costs?


Standby removes idle compute. A sandbox that suspends when its connection closes stops billing for CPU and memory and charges only for snapshot and volume storage until the next session. TTL expiration removes abandoned sandboxes entirely, along with their snapshotbut any separate snapshots may outlive the sandbox and continue consuming storage unless they expire or are deleted under the provider’s snapshot policy. Together the two policies mean you pay for the time agents actually execute, not for environments engineers forgot to shut down after a test.


### What should I monitor in a coding agent sandbox?


Monitor process execution, blocked egress attempts, tool calls, and resource spikes, all captured from outside the guest so an attacker inside can't disable collection. Build a per-task baseline for call volume and process trees, then alert on deviations rather than on raw thresholds. Store the logs in write-once storage so the forensic timeline survives even if the sandbox itself is compromised or deleted.


### Does a SOC 2 sandbox provider make my agent SOC 2 compliant?


No. The provider's SOC 2 report covers the controls it operates: isolation, infrastructure logging, access to the platform. Your agent's scope is still yours. That covers how you grant tools, where you store customer data, who can change prompts, and incident response. A certified provider shrinks the controls you must build and document, which shortens your audit. It doesn't replace your own program.
